speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND TO PROVIDE BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will be fairly brief in dealing with some matters I feel are related to the bill before us. I want to speak about the principles contained within the act, the principles of taxation and the way in which taxes, once having been collected, are redistributed in our society.
I cannot recall an occasion when I have walked on the streets of Hamilton when someone has not come to me and said he was vitally concerned about both the level of taxation at the personal income tax level and, more importantly, about the way the government goes about spending the money it raises. Everyone has his own hobbyhorse, of course; everyone has his own area in which he feels the government is perhaps misdirecting his funds. People are expressing a frustration every day about the apparent desire of the government to continue to not only raise money, which I think we all understand is necessary, but over how the government determines its priorities in the expenditure of many of the dollars which are so difficult to come by for private individuals.
I was looking at a chart the other day which shows a dramatic turnaround in the balance of the total tax burden carried by the personal income tax sector over and against the corporate tax sector. Although the figures themselves may not be as meaningful, indeed, when you look at them in detail, as they are when you look at them baldly, they are still rather startling.
In 1980 the percentage of total government revenue raised from personal income tax will be 37 per cent while the percentage raised from the corporate tax will be 10.3 per cent. When you look at that over and against the situation which prevailed in 1950, you find that in 1950 the percentage of expenditures raised from personal income tax was 20 per cent while the percentage raised from corporate tax was 22.5 per cent. You have to ask yourself what has happened in society because we have moved the burden of taxation so dramatically from the corporate sector to the private taxpayer. We must ask what has happened in society that has required us to place such an onerous burden, particularly on the low and middle-income taxpayers, taking out of their income such a substantial amount of money at a time when that money might will be better used to purchase goods and services within the community and thereby creating an expanded economy that would enable the corporate sector, if I might say it, to pay a larger share of the over-all tax burden than it is presently paying, because it would be receiving considerably more of the expenditure moneys of the total population.
Income Tax Act
One cannot help wonder, and I wonder along with many of the people I represent, about the expenditures of government. People have reluctantly become accustomed to carrying the burden of inadequate government management. They have expressed, and I think quite rightly so, that the government does not do a very good job of managing. I think this is primarily because the governments which have been in power have had very natural tendencies to be reluctant to be managers of the economy. Governments do not see themselves in that role. They do not see that they have a responsibility to manage the economy, not only the tax area of the economy I am speaking of now, but the economy in general, and to have a say in the direction the economy will go and to have some influence on the final decisions which are made that so much affect the day to day lives of the people.
People are becoming increasingly aware that they are also having to carry the burden of inadequate corporate management through the tax structure. We have to look very seriously at that problem. It is bad enough that the average taxpayer, the low and middle-income taxpayer, the people who work in plants and can hardly make ends meet, should have to carry the burden daily of the government's stupidity, but that they should also now in this new evolving society have to carry the burden of inadequate corporate decisions through their tax structure is unconscionable. That is what we are seeing happening. On a day to day basis we see the corporate sector awakening to the new idea that it can come to government any time things go wrong and the government, under pressure, will have to hand out more and more tax dollars, primarily because of the inadequacy of the management of the corporations involved. Corporations have found a new method of funding their failures. It is not only becoming more common for small businesses to cry, and 1 think quite rightly so, that they are mistreated and having difficulty making it in the marketplace because of a very severely restricted economy, but the giants of the industrial sector are lining up one behind the other, unashamedly reaching into the public trough in order to finance their inadequate management decisions which have resulted in failures.
It is very difficult for me to rationalize with the people I represent that they should be burdened on a day to day business with giving handouts to the corporate giants of this world without their having some say in the decisions being made with respect to the futures of those corporate giants. That is the nub of the problem.
When I read the Income Tax Act and look at the suggestions being made, all I can see is a perpetuation of an existing inadequate and unfair system. I cannot express adequately how much I feel the injustice of what is happening in this society. It appears to me that bad management is to be rewarded and that people on the side of good management with foresight, good reinvestment policy and adequate labour relations policy seem to be asked to carry more and more of the burden, along with the average taxpayers of this country. The Chryslers come knocking on the door. The Massey-Fergu-

January 19, 1981
Income Tax Act
sons come knocking on the door. There are so many of them it becomes impossible because, as we begin to look at them, we find companies which for years decried the management of government. They told government to stay out of their business. They said that government knew nothing about management and that they, the Chryslers, the Masseys and the others, were the people who knew how to operate in the marketplace.
Yet if we stop and look, we find that they knew nothing about how to operate in the marketplace. They did not know how to manage the businesses they were managing, and they are not alone. The problem with which we are faced is that we have to raise more and more money, not only to subsidize failures but also in order to maintain communities and families which are devastated by the stupidity of the corporations of which I speak. This is a cause for great concern, and I wish more people in this House would give some consideration to what really is happening in this society.
On the one hand, Chrysler is attempting to gain favour with the government in order to try to put back on the tracks a company which has been run into the ground. If we say no, we doom a great number of employees to very serious hardship. If we say yes, then we invite others in the field to line up at the door of the treasury building in order that they too can gain access to the same public funding, and in order that they too can have their bad management decisions funded at public expense. I think this is a cause for alarm. It is a fairly new phenomenon. Ten years ago one rarely, if ever, heard of major corporations knocking at the door of the government for handouts.
That has become a normal practice today, and what concerns me is that we are dealing with this in such a piecemeal fashion that the bottom line of the bill we will have to pay will in the final analysis far exceed the number of tax dollars we will be able to pull in through corporate tax. Eventually we will end up paying out more than we will be able to get back.
We must get a clear picture of what is really going on in this society. Why is it that in private lending institutions there is not an apparent desire to take some risks? It is their business to take some risks in the refinancing, redevelopment and reindustrialization which inevitably must take place in order to relieve taxpayers all across this country who, frankly, cannot afford at this point in time to fund out of their own tax dollars what in essence is the bad decision-making of a few individuals who are, incidentally, still running companies and still making decisions, which will again come back to haunt us. There are some serious problems here and, in looking at taxation and the distribution of taxation, the government will be required to look very long and hard at the kinds of programs which are introduced to try to accommodate the greed which I think has probably been in place over the last two or three decades and which has extracted from consumers substantial amounts, more than consumers ought to have been required to pay.
Having extracted that money, this greed has resulted in a refusal to put sufficient amounts back into the companies involved so that they could maintain levels of productivity and
technology which would have kept them in the forefront of the struggle for adequate and reasonably low cost commodities.
Today I went to a press conference held by three government ministers. Those ministers were telling my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and me, together with the press, how they will spend another $350 million of taxpayers' money. They will spend $175 million of that $350 million on a number of grant programs and subsidization programs for workers who are dislocated as a result of the bad management decisions to which 1 have referred. Over the next three years, they will spend $175 million assisting in the redevelopment of the very companies and others which, by the very terms of reference of these programs, have also made bad management decisions. I must ask myself whether this kind of program is of any value to this country now or in the future. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will address that problem tomorrow afternoon.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AID-CONSIDERATION OF TRIPARTITE AID TO THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES
EXTERNAL AID-CONSIDERATION OF TRIPARTITE AID TO THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are well aware that a large part of our foreign aid budget is transferred directly from Canada to the poorly developed countries in a form called bilateral aid.
Similarly, people are well aware that more aid is transferred to multinational organizations like the United Nations, called multilateral aid. A less common form of aid which encompasses almost none of the budget for foreign aid from Canada is in the form of trilateral or tripartite aid. Trilateral or
January 19, 1981

tripartite aid is not a new suggestion. It is only new in the sense that it has been brought forward in the North-South program for survival, the Brandt report.
In many cases you will find that there are all kinds of conferences and all kinds of reports such as the North-South dialogue, the Canadian House of Commons North-South Relations report, the report of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who was skiing in the Alps, and so on, but when you get right down to it, so often all these reports evaporate like so much hot air because they contain so little substance, so little that is specific on what we might do to actually make the improvements that are required in the developing and the developed countries. One specific idea which was brought forward in the Brandt report is excellent. As I read it, I knew who it was meant for because it related to Canada. I should like to read from page 140 of the Brandt report a passage which reads as follows:
The emergence of capital surplus developing countries provides special scope for the establishment of projects on a basis of tripartite arrangements involving developing countries alone or in partnership with industrialized countries. Such arrangements should be supported by both developed and developing countries. Tripartite projects, including, when appropriate, industrialized countries, should be encouraged by nations with complementary resources such as capital and technology.
Our Prime Minister travelled through Saudi Arabia, a country with surplus petro dollars which, in fact, they had to recycle. That nation is known for its contributions to developing nations, specifically through bilateral aid.
But in addition to bilateral aid, there is another opportunity here. While Saudi Arabia has surplus capital, Canada has a great capacity for technological aid exchange. In addition to that, our plants can manufacture and produce surplus goods. So why should we not take the capital of Saudi Arabia and our capacity to produce goods and technological aid, put those two together and transfer them to a third country like Somalia?
In my question to the minister, I made a specific suggestion. The idea I suggested is that we combine the capital of Saudi Arabia with our technological capacity in so far as energy is concerned. In fact, Canada has just set up Enertech, a new corporation, which will do substantial work in research into our resources. Why should we not have Enertech together with CIDA and the capital of Saudi Arabia or that of another OPEC nation provide an exchange to a needy country like Somalia? Somalia is the fourth poorest country in the world with the most massive refugee problem in the world. Can we not, for example, transfer our solar energy technology to that country? We produce solar energy water pumps. The most basic element of life is water. Canada has the capacity to provide the pumps to bring out water from underground. Some nations are already doing it. Why not pump that water from the ground in Somalia, not only to provide water for the people but to provide water for their crops so that they can become more self-sufficient? Here is another kernel of an idea. As a Member of Parliament you wonder about these things, you have ideas and you bring them forward in the House of Commons.
Adjournment Debate
The minister says that he will certainly be prepared to give serious consideration to that proposal. That was November 16. The minister has had time for consideration. The Prime Minister has been to Saudi Arabia. He has been to undeveloped countries. There is no excuse to not move beyond the rhetoric, beyond the North-South dialogue and have that measured in some real and tangible way by Canada. Here is a specific idea. What must I do to have the government take an idea like this? It is not my own idea. It is an idea resulting from a great deal of study in the North-South report. Why do they not take this idea and in a real way measure the success of all these reports? That success is when the kernel of grain reaches the stomach or the soil of that Third World nation, which is poor and needy.
I hope that as a result of having raised this question here tonight in this House of Commons that maybe I will have touched a nerve or chord somewhere in a member or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) on the other side of the House. I hope it will not be given some kind of passing, fleeting response but that it will be given consideration.
I brought forth the case of Somalia here in the House of Commons and also in committee. Others have done the same. What must we do to get through to the bureaucracy to tell them we have found a problem? We have found a need of the people to receive, not just this form of aid, but bilateral aid as well, to be identified as a country. Why can we not take the need td receive and connect it with our capacity as a nation to give and to share? I challenge the government with that tonight.

subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF COMMUNITY SERVICES CONTRIBUTION PROGRAM
MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF COMMUNITY SERVICES CONTRIBUTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15 I put a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), who is responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, concerning the community services program. I asked this question of him because he recently announced that in 1982 he would be ceasing this program, which has been providing some $250 million per year of assistance to municipalities for municipal infrastructure for housing programs, community improvement programs and so on.
I have had a number of representations from municipalities in my constituency which are very concerned with the termination of this program. They are especially concerned in two communities in my constituency where there are projects which are already committed, where the project has been tendered and where a contract has been let. So, for these communities which so far have no definite commitment from the government, it is a matter of great concern.
One project is the $4 million sewer and water infrastructure project for Little Current, to which the Community Services Contribution Program was to provide $1.29 million. Another project is with regard to the new community development in Elliot Lake at a cost of some $29.9 million, of which the Community Services Contribution Program was to provide funding in the amount of $4.6 million. It was to be used for this rapidly expanding community where the funds are urgently required.
What I would like to know from the minister tonight is whether or not the province of Ontario has recommended these two projects. I understand that the cut-off date for the projects to be recommended by the province of Ontario is February 5. I am interested to know whether the two projects have been recommended, and are included in the funds allocated for the province of Ontario over the next couple of years.
There is no question that these funds and the projects are urgently needed for the communities. In the case of Little Current, the projects are needed for reasons of sanitation and the municipal infrastructure. In the case of Elliot Lake, the project is needed due to the massive expansion of this town, because of the uranium mining industry in that community, over the next four years or five years. When this program was put in place, these projects were planned. The projects were tendered and the contracts have been let, so the Community Services Contribution Program is a major funding instrument to these communities. Both communities will be placed in a catastrophic position financially if the money, totalling some $6 million for both communities, is not made available.
I hope the minister will be able to respond and indicate that the province of Ontario has recommended these two projects for funding under the Community Services Contribution Program and that the federal government is now prepared to extend this program for at least another year so that these projects may be completed and the benefits can accrue to the community and as a result to the entire country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF COMMUNITY SERVICES CONTRIBUTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond further to the question raised on December 15 by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) concerning the termination of the Community Services Contribution Program. The decision not to renew the program was a difficult one, and I would like to take this opportunity to outline the factors which contributed to the government's decision.
First, there was the question of whether it was appropriate for the federal government to continue funding the provision of services which, from a jurisdictional point of view, have been the responsibility of the provinces and the municipalities. It is not a matter of whether the program was good, but rather, who should pay for such a program. Second, there is the issue of accountability, whether the government responsible for raising resources through taxation should not also be responsible for the expenditures of such revenues. Third, the effectiveness of the program was analysed from the point of view of job generation and compared with other programs that demonstrate a better return from money spent.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the present climate of fiscal restraint contributed to this decision. In meeting the objective of providing more effective government, the continuation of existing programs has been studied with a view to providing funds for new programs or those of a higher priority. The decision not to renew the Community Services Contribution Program now results in more funds being available for addressing higher priorities in the fiscal year 1982-83. The task remains to determine precisely the federal housing priorities in the 1980s. The minister will continue to hold informal discussions with his provincial counterparts and with other interested groups on this matter. It is his hope that this will assist in developing federal housing priorities and programs and lead to the best distribution funds between them.
Under the Community Services Contribution Program, the federal government has allocated a total of $400 million for municipal projects, $150 million of which was for the 1979 program year and $250 million of which was for the 1980 program year.
Over 3,000 projects in some 1,000 communities will have received federal assistance. This is a significant contribution to the provision of local services to Canadians in every province.
The minister wishes to assure the hon. member that the government will meet all commitments under the present federal-provincial community services contribution agreements. As the hon. member is aware, concerns have been

raised about the time committed for the use of the 1980 program year funds. The funding is scheduled to terminate at the end of March, 1982. However, the minister is seeking an extension of that date, to enable communities to have the time to incur the necessary expenditures. He is confident that this extension will be granted, on the understanding that fiscal expenditures in 1981-82 will be reduced to reflect expenditures to be made in 1982-83.
I do not have specific answers about the two projects the hon. member has referred to, but 1 am sure the minister will be able to provide him with that information.

subtopic: GRAIN-REIMBURSEMENT OF PRODUCERS FOR LOSS OF INCOME FROM DEPRESSED PRICES
GRAIN-REIMBURSEMENT OF PRODUCERS FOR LOSS OF INCOME FROM DEPRESSED PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, more than seven months ago I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question:
Will the Prime Minister fulfil his promise to reimburse grain producers for their loss of income so that some extra cash can be injected into the drought-ridden farm economy?
The Prime Minister's answer on June 2 last year was that the matter "is being considered". At this time, seven months and seventeen days later, compensation for farmers who suffered income losses due to the grain embargo is still being considered.
As late as December 10 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in an answer indicated as follows:
As far as I am concerned, we intend to live up to what we have said. As I said the other day in the House, we do not intend to welsh on any agreement made by the previous government; this is one we said we would fulfil.
It is good to see that the government is progressing after seven months, but 1 think all hon. members present tonight will admit that the progress is pretty slow. Let us review for a moment where we stand in terms of embargo losses.
The embargo was put in place on January 4 last year as co-operation with the U.S. in their action to protest Soviet action in Afghanistan. The embargoing of 17 million tonnes of U.S. grain immediately depressed Canadian prices of food and feed grains. Countries which sold into the Soviet market received as much as $50 per tonne more than the prices quoted in countries observing the embargo.
All of this added up to substantial losses for the Canadian Wheat Board which was forced to operate as an arm of federal government policy. This is very significant, because the Canadian Wheat Board is funded by farmers of Canada to sell, as is stated in the charter, "the most wheat at the best price". What we have is an agency, funded by the farmers, selling the farmers short.
We can imagine that the farmers of Canada were upset and that most members of Parliament were upset, including western Conservatives such as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) who brought this matter up in the House. During that period we had a delightful bit of fancy footwork by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, Senator Argue, who said it was keeping up normal and traditional
Adjournment Debate
levels of sales. Those sales vary from 3 million tonnes to 3.3 million tonnes to 3.5 million tonnes, as the sales increased.
On the other hand, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) insisted that this elastic band embargo still meant restrictions on the amount Canada would sell the Soviets until even he changed his position and decided that the government could not agree to restraints at the United States level, but the damage had been done. By not aggressively selling wheat into the Soviet markets, we lost premiums, and we almost lost the market. The Soviet market is where we sell the best grades of wheat. We also lost a good deal of money, an amount which the federal government has calculated several times but has failed to disclose.
In this year, when we are supposed to have freedom of information, Liberal style, I believe that we have arrived at 1984 three years in advance. We are not getting any information. I suggest that the government is doing very well in the "new-speak" department when, on the one hand, the government insists that compensation is going to be paid, that it is very much on its mind, but on the other hand it gives no inkling of how much the government intends to pay.
Many of us believe that the government will try to slip a nominal amount in between the 1979-1980 crop year final payments, which were announced on January 8, and the interim payments which will be announced at the end of the month. I would welcome any guarantees from the government side that this will not be the case. Luckily, we have had some public guidance as to the losses.
The University of Saskatchewan brought forward a study about the middle of July. That study showed the losses were $117 million for wheat and $9 million for barley for the period January to June last year. This amounted to 50 cents a bushel for wheat, approximately $1,200 for each of the 150,000 permit holders in the west. This would be welcome payment to many farmers who not only have to look at their staggering bank interest, but who have to put in next year's crop and feed cattle now at very high prices.
I want to ask the government the same questions again: when is the government going to pay compensation; how much and how did it arrive at the rate?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GRAIN-REIMBURSEMENT OF PRODUCERS FOR LOSS OF INCOME FROM DEPRESSED PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to compensation, as I advised the House last Tuesday evening in answer to a similar question, the government is considering the question of compensation to producers for losses attributable to the partial embargo on grain to the U.S.S.R. A report on this subject has been prepared by officials and is now before the ministers for an early determination.
When the question was asked on June 2, the hon. member referred to the drought situation then prevailing in the west, along with cash flow problems being experienced by producers.
As all hon. members are aware, the situation has improved significantly since June. For example, in June the international

January 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
price for No. 1 Canada western Red Spring wheat in store Thunder Bay was $197.56 per tonne or $5.38 per bushel. The comparable figure last Friday was $269.62 per tonne or $7.34 per bushel. That is an increase of almost $2 per bushel in seven months. Prices of other grains and oil seeds are also up sharply. Exports are running at a level above the record established a year ago, and this large movement is reflected in producers' deliveries and consequently in cash returns to producers.
In July the government announced higher initial payments for the current crop year, and before Christmas the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board indicated, on December 16, that he expected to announce a further increase in initial payments early in 1981, possibly near the beginning of February.
Hon. members will also be aware of the final payments of the 1979-80 wheat and barley pools which were announced on January 9. The minister noted that the final payments will
amount to a total cash flow of more than $730 million to the prairie economy, with about $446.8 million going to Saskatchewan, about $187.3 million to Alberta and the Peace River area of British Columbia and about $96.4 million to Manitoba. The board will this week begin mailing over 336,000 final payment cheques to prairie producers.
As I said on Tuesday evening, to the extent that actual loss can be determined, the western producer can expect to be compensated in the near future. Determination of the amount is a complex problem. The hon. member mentioned the University of Saskatchewan study which indicated a $126 million loss, and the Conservatives last Tuesday said that the loss was $75 million. Government experts also have an evaluation which will be announced when the compensation is announced.
